136.0.0.en: O give thanks unto the LORD, for He is good, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.0.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm calls all the believers in the whole world, throughout the generations, to give thanks to God because He is good, and it is His nature to do good with all His creatures, and especially those who believe in Him, so He supports them in their weakness and rescues them from their enemies and satisfies them with His good things.

136.0.2.en: 2- The writer of the psalm reminds those who praise that God's mercy is not only on the earth, as appears from this psalm, but extends for ever in the Kingdom of Heaven with gifts and blessings that surpass the mind, which the tongue cannot express.

136.1.0.en: O give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy endures for ever. O give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.1.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm calls the whole world to thank and give thanks to God, the God of gods. What is meant by gods is everyone whose strength and authority people feel, whether of men such as kings and rulers (Ps 82:6; Jn 10:34) or those who claim to be gods, which are the idols (Dan 2:47); He is above all power and authority, and He alone is the true God, able to show mercy on the earth and for ever.

136.1.2.en: 2- Thanks is also offered to God because He is Lord of lords, and what is meant by lords is all the great creatures in heaven, that is, the great ranks of angels who have authority; God is also their Creator and their Lord, that is, their master and father, and He alone is able to show mercy on the earth and in heaven.

136.1.3.en: God's good things toward you are many, so it is natural for you to thank Him for them. And when you become accustomed to thanksgiving every day, God will open your spiritual eyes, and you will see and discover His works, His care, and His love for you more clearly, and your joy will increase.

136.2.0.en: To Him who alone does great wonders, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him that by wisdom made the heavens, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him that stretched out the earth above the waters, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him that made great lights, for His mercy endures for ever. The sun to rule by day, for His mercy endures for ever. The moon and stars to rule by night, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.2.1.en: 1- God alone is the Creator, and He made everything of the creatures great and small, and here he recounts a group of His great works, which are the heaven and the earth, the sun, the moon and the stars, as examples of His creatures, and from their creation the extent of His greatness appears. The psalm calls them wonders because God's power and His plans appear in them, which surpass the human mind, and by this the psalm protects the person chanting from deviating after any pagan gods, all of which are worthless, because God alone is able to create.

136.2.2.en: 2- The heavens and the creatures in them, that is, the angels, are above man's comprehension, and he knows only a little about them. All of these God created by understanding, that is, by wisdom that surpasses the mind.

136.2.3.en: 3- God's wonderful work in spreading the earth upon the waters, as the oceans surround it on every side. For the earth, although it turns on itself and around the sun, is firm, to give stability to the life of man.

136.2.4.en: 4- God also created the sun to declare the hours of the day on the earth, because the earth turns once on itself every day, so it is lit by the light of the sun for about half the day, or more, while the other half, which is called night, it is lit by the light of the moon and the stars. Therefore the sun rules and arranges the hours of the day, and the moon and stars rule and arrange the hours of the night. All this by the arrangement of the great Creator, God alone.

136.2.5.en: 5- All that is mentioned in these verses is mentioned in the Book of Genesis in the order of the days of creation (Gen 1:6-18).

136.2.6.en: If you meditate on nature you will feel the greatness of God who created everything for your sake, so you glorify Him and thank Him at the same time for His love for you, and your heart is reassured, because God, who is able to do everything, loves you and protects you.

136.3.0.en: To Him that smote Egypt in their firstborn, for His mercy endures for ever. And brought out Israel from among them, for His mercy endures for ever. With a strong hand and with a stretched out arm, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him who divided the Red Sea into parts, for His mercy endures for ever. And made Israel to pass through the midst of it, for His mercy endures for ever. But overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red Sea, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.3.1.en: 1- After God showed His work in which He is alone, which is creation, he speaks here of His rescue of His people the children of Israel from the slavery of Egypt. And here appears His making men and angels share with Him in His great works, to the end of the chapter; for God loves His creatures and encourages them, and even ascribes to them some of His glories.

136.3.2.en: 2- He refers here to His wonders in Egypt for the rescue of His people, which are the ten plagues, and he concentrates on the tenth plague, which is the killing of the firstborn of the Egyptians, because of which Pharaoh yielded and permitted the children of Israel to go out of Egypt, though this yielding was temporary, because he returned in the hardness of his heart and went out after them to bring them back again to slavery, so God destroyed him.

136.3.3.en: 3- God rescued His people from Pharaoh by dividing the Red Sea into parts, that is, sections, and we understand from the Holy Bible that He opened a way in the Red Sea (the Sea of Suph). The waters were on both sides like a wall on the right and on the left, and this is a wonderful work the like of which had not been heard before. And when Pharaoh dared to follow the children of Israel, God drowned them in the Red Sea after His people were saved and went out to the wilderness of Sinai.

136.3.4.en: 4- The crossing of the Red Sea signifies Baptism, and the rod of Moses with which he struck the sea signifies the Cross. And by the children of Israel crossing the Red Sea they were rid of the slavery of Pharaoh, who signifies Satan. And the drowning of Pharaoh and his soldiers signifies the death of the old man, that is, the nature inclined to evil, in the waters of Baptism.

136.3.5.en: 5- God's power was not only in dividing the Red Sea, but also in supporting His children, for He gave them courage to cross through the water to the other shore, that is, the wilderness of Sinai. And the pillar of fire protected them from behind and separated them from Pharaoh and his soldiers.

136.4.0.en: To Him who led His people through the wilderness, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him who smote great kings, for His mercy endures for ever. And slew famous kings, for His mercy endures for ever. Sihon king of the Amorites, for His mercy endures for ever. And Og the king of Bashan, for His mercy endures for ever. And gave their land for an heritage, for His mercy endures for ever. Even an heritage unto Israel His servant, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.4.1.en: 1- The psalm tells us in these verses of God's care for His people in the wilderness of Sinai, and He brought them into the land of Canaan; He Himself was their leader, and walked with them in the wilderness forty years, and He led them by the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night, and God sustained them with food and drink, and kept them from their enemies such as Amalek, until He brought them to the east of the land of Canaan.

136.4.2.en: 2- On the way of the children of Israel to Canaan they met great kings and killed them by the power of God, and he mentions among them as examples Sihon and Og, who were distinguished by strength and the fortification of their cities and their wealth, and they are the ones who opposed the children of Israel during their crossing. These kings signify Satan who opposes God's children, and God gives them victory over him.

136.4.3.en: 3- God gave the land of the pagan kings to the children of Israel, to be an inheritance for them. What is meant by the land is the souls that worship paganism, which believed in Christ in the fullness of time and became the people of God, that is, the Christians; and what is also meant is the places of the demons who fell from heaven, which are received by the human beings who believe in Christ, and so become an everlasting possession for them in the Kingdom of Heaven.

136.5.0.en: Who remembered us in our low estate, for His mercy endures for ever. And has redeemed us from our enemies, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.5.1.en: God's fatherhood and tenderness appear in His feeling for His people, whom Pharaoh humiliated and enslaved and forced to work cruelly, so they cried out to God in humility, asking His help, and He intervened and rescued them and brought them out of Egypt by the hand of Moses. The one who humiliates man is Satan and sin, but repentance and prayer rescue man from every affliction.

136.6.0.en: Who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.6.1.en: The psalm closes with thanks to God who feeds all people, Jews and Gentiles, and also the righteous and the wicked. He cares for all, to establish the righteous in their righteousness, and to call the wicked in His love to repentance and faith in Him. Indeed He also feeds the animals and birds and plants and trees, for He is the source of life for all His living creatures.

136.7.0.en: O give thanks to the God of heaven, for His mercy endures for ever.

136.7.1.en: And at the end he calls everyone to thank the God of heaven, so as to lift their eyes to their eternal future, that they may live with God in His fear, and believe in Him and keep His commandments, and so His mercies toward them increase all their days.

136.7.2.en: Lift your eyes, my brother, toward heaven every morning, that you may walk this day in a manner worthy of the heavenly ones, and so enjoy God's care and fellowship, and prepare for the Kingdom of Heaven with energy and zeal.

136.7.3.en: The longing of the captives for Jerusalem. “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down ...” (v. 1). Introduction:

136.7.4.en: 1- Its writer: there is more than one opinion:

136.7.5.en: a- It is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is not known, because the name of the writer is not mentioned in the title of the psalm.

136.7.6.en: b- It is David, as is found in the title of the psalm in the Septuagint translation; he wrote it in the spirit of prophecy about the Babylonian captivity and its end.

136.7.7.en: c- It is written in the title of the Septuagint translation “Of David, for Jeremiah,” that is, David wrote it for Jeremiah to repeat it at the destruction of Babylon. Some see that its writer is Jeremiah himself, who lived at the time of the Babylonian captivity and its end.

136.7.8.en: d- It is one of the Levites of the captivity who returned to Jerusalem in the first return with Zerubbabel.

136.7.9.en: 2- When was it written? There is also more than one opinion:

136.7.10.en: a- The days of David if the writer is David, and he wrote in the spirit of prophecy about the events of the captivity and the destruction of Babylon.

136.7.11.en: b- It was written during the Babylonian captivity, and the last part of the psalm (vv. 7-9) was written in the spirit of prophecy about what would happen to Babylon of destruction.

136.7.12.en: c- It was written a short time after the return from captivity.

136.7.13.en: 3- This psalm suits everyone who feels his exile in the world and his longing for the heavenly Jerusalem. It also suits every penitent who rejects the slavery of sin and longs for life with Christ.

136.7.14.en: 4- This psalm can be considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it prophesies about Christ in the last verse.

136.7.15.en: 5- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, to lift our longings to the Kingdom of Heaven.

137.0.0.en: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down; yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.

137.0.1.en: 1- These are the feelings of the captives in Babylon, who sat on the banks of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and all the canals branching from them. They remembered Jerusalem and the temple of God, and wept for the loss of worship in the temple. Although their appearance was restful on the banks of the rivers, their sorrow of heart was great, for the loss of the most important thing, which is being with God and worshiping Him, especially since Babylon signifies evil throughout the history of the Holy Bible, because of its being filled with many lusts, and that from the days of the tower of Babel (Gen 11:9) to the end of the Holy Bible in the Book of Revelation (Rev 17:1-6).

137.0.2.en: 2- Sitting on the rivers, that is, their banks, signifies those attached to the world, but they are better than those who went down into the rivers to swim in them, who signify those immersed in lusts.

137.0.3.en: 3- Perhaps those sitting on the rivers who remembered the temple also remembered their brethren the captives, who forgot Jerusalem and were occupied with trade and building houses and left God, indeed entered into the worship of idols, so they wept for them, asking God to awaken them to return to Him.

137.1.0.en: We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst of it.

137.1.1.en: Willows: trees widespread in Syria that grow along watercourses, and they are shade trees, that is, they have leaves and many branches, and have no fruit, and their leaves are pyramid-shaped and their edges are serrated like a saw.

137.1.2.en: 1- The captives sat in the shade of the willow trees on the rivers of Babylon, and hung their harps on these trees. Although they had brought them out of Judea because of their attachment to singing to God, they could not praise in a foreign land, and their slavery to Babylon made them aware of their bondage, so they hung up the harps because of their lack of desire to praise away from the temple, of which they were deprived, and they did not break the harps because of their hope of returning to Jerusalem, that is, Zion.

137.1.3.en: 2- The willow is a tree without fruit, so it signifies the person without spiritual fruits, who is unable to praise God, and one who is in the slavery of sin, his tongue is not loosed in praise.

137.2.0.en: For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song, and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, “Sing us one of the songs of Zion.”

137.2.1.en: 1- The captives were in sorrow and weeping because of their distance from Jerusalem, and the Babylonians asked them to sing the songs of Zion, famous for their beautiful melodies, and the captives were very astonished, and felt that they could not sing in a foreign land, because the worship of God by singing is offered only in the temple of Jerusalem. In addition, their souls were in sorrow, and utterly far from delighting in beautiful melodies, and their whole feeling was longing to return to Jerusalem.

137.2.2.en: 2- The penitent who grieves over his sins finds it hard to take delight in the joys of the world and its lusts, for weeping over his sins and rejecting evil suit him.

137.2.3.en: 3- The Babylonians who enslaved the children of Israel and tormented them humiliated them when they asked them, while they were in sorrow and weeping, to sing songs of joy, but this humiliation increased the captives' longings for Jerusalem to offer worship there, as appears from the following verses (vv. 4-6).

137.2.4.en: Take care to examine yourself every day to repent of your sins and to discover the sources of evil that made you fall, and keep away from them. And when you offer repentance before God and confess your sins before the priest you receive peace, and an inclination to a new beginning with God.

137.3.0.en: How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?

137.3.1.en: 1- The captives could not sing to God in a foreign land, because the songs of worship are offered only in the temple of Jerusalem.

137.3.2.en: 2- Singing in Babylon refers to offering holy things and speaking of them in the council of mockers, or before those who do not appreciate their value; we ought not to cast holy things and pearls before any stranger, for he does not understand them, and may despise them for his lack of understanding.

137.3.3.en: 3- Jerusalem signifies the deep spiritual life, and the foreign land signifies distance from God. And one who is far from God cannot praise Him, even if he has the instruments of praise such as harps, that is, even if his voice is beautiful and his ability to perform songs is outstanding, yet he does not feel the feelings of praise to God, so his praises are a superficial outward performance, and do not reach God.

137.4.0.en: If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget! Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth, if I remember you not, if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy!

137.4.1.en: 1- The captive says that if he forgets Jerusalem his right hand will forget, that is, his hand will be unable to play the musical instrument, and also if his tongue does not repeat what expresses his love for Jerusalem, his tongue will be unable to speak ordinarily with people, and therefore cannot sing to take delight in melodies with worldly delight. And this shows the extent of his heart's attachment to Jerusalem and the worship of God in His temple, so he cannot be occupied with the lusts of the world and its pleasures.

137.4.2.en: 2- Although the captive, as a man, has what gladdens him of the material things of the world, that is, food and clothing and possessions, his joy in God and His worship rises very far above the joys of the world; his joy in God is greater than everything, and his whole heart is occupied with God.

137.4.3.en: Remember with every morning the words of Christ, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” so that you give yourself a great opportunity for prayer and being with God, and remember Him also during your many works and preoccupations.

137.5.0.en: Remember, O LORD, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who said, “Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation of it.”

137.5.1.en: 1- The captive felt in his weakness and humiliation that he had no hope but God, so he lifted his eyes to Him, asking Him to deal with those who torment him. He did not mention Babylon only, but asked still more for Edom, who are the neighbors of the Jews living south of their land, and they are the descendants of Esau, that is, relatives of the Jews.

137.5.2.en: These were in intense enmity with the children of Israel, and gloated over them at the attack of Babylon on them, and during their demolition of Jerusalem and its walls they were encouraging the Babylonians to demolish the walls, until the foundation was torn up so that Jerusalem would be utterly ruined, its temple and its palaces and its walls.

137.5.3.en: 2- Edom signifies the demons who rejoice and fight the righteous, and want to destroy them completely, and remove their foundation, which is Christ, from their hearts. And Edom means red; therefore it signifies Satan, the shedder of blood.

137.6.0.en: O daughter of Babylon, who are to be destroyed, happy shall he be that rewards you as you have served us!

137.6.1.en: 1- Here he calls on Edom, which helped Babylon in seizing the Jews and selling them as slaves during the Babylonian attack on Jerusalem. And he calls her the daughter of Babylon, for she is her daughter in evil, and he asks God to declare His justice, so that Edom receives her recompense, so that the righteous may stand firm in their faith, and the wicked repent, and not be dazzled by the power of evil; it is not gloating on the part of the Jews, but holding fast to divine justice.

137.6.2.en: 2- The spiritual man calls on his wretched soul, the daughter of Babylon in evil, which made him fall into sin and took him far from God, and he repays it with fasting and spiritual striving. And as it took him far from God, he repays it with the same recompense, that is, he brings it back forcefully to God in repentance, that it may live with Him anew.

137.7.0.en: Happy shall he be that takes and dashes your little ones against the rock!

137.7.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm continues his words about Edom, and blesses those whom God used to punish Edom, who are Abishai the commander of the army in the days of David, who threw the Edomites from a high rock in the Valley of Salt, and they perished (1 Chr 18:12). And also King Amaziah killed 10,000 of the Edomites and took another 10,000 of them and threw them from the top of Selah, and they fell and were broken (2 Chr 25:11, 12).

137.7.2.en: 2- The children of the Edomites signify the sins of God's children who repent, so they dash their lusts and evils against the rock, who is Christ, that they may be broken and removed from them, and they live in purity by the power of Christ the Savior.

137.7.3.en: Do not keep company with the wicked, or walk in their way, lest you be defiled and fall into their sins, but cut off your relationship with them firmly, whatever the cost, and hasten to repentance, for your Christ awaits you to purify you, and you will live in purity and peace with Him.

137.7.4.en: Thanksgiving to God for His fatherhood to David. “I will praise You with my whole heart; before the gods I will sing praises to You” (v. 1). Introduction:

137.7.5.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, as appears in the title of the psalm in the Hebrew text that is in our hands. It is noticed that in the Septuagint translation the title mentions “Of Haggai and Zechariah” or “Of Zechariah” after the name of David. This means that Haggai and Zechariah used to repeat this psalm after the return from captivity, but the meaning of this is that the writer is David. And the words of this psalm resemble the psalms of David.

137.7.6.en: 2- When was it written? After David's great victories over the surrounding enemies, that is, it was in the last part of David's life.

137.7.7.en: 3- This psalm expresses David's deep feelings toward God, and his experiences of God's power in afflictions.

137.7.8.en: 4- This psalm suits everyone who loves God, or thanks Him for His gifts, so his faith increases and is established during afflictions.

137.7.9.en: 5- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms that speak clearly of the Incarnation of the Word, which is the greatest declaration and manifestation of God to people, to make Himself known to them and save them from their sins.

137.7.10.en: 6- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, to encourage us to thank God for His works with us all day long, and especially in distress.
